column1: Reconstruct the dreaming argument (Med. 1).
column2:
Aim: show that the senses cannot certify any judgment about particular bodies.
Premises: I have often had experiences in sleep exactly like this one; "there are no certain indications by which we may clearly distinguish wakefulness from sleep" (Med. 1, AT VII 19); so I may now be dreaming, and my sensory judgment may be false.
Conclusion: no sensory judgment about particular bodies is certain. Arithmetic survives (AT VII 20), so a second argument is needed.
Objection: it undermines itself, since knowing that past dreams deceived me needs the mark it denies (Austin); Malcolm denies that dreams are experiences.
Reply (the literature's): it needs only the possibility that this is a dream (Williams, Stroud). Descartes' own answer, coherence backed by God's veracity (Med. 6, AT VII 89), inherits Argument 7's trouble.

column1: Reconstruct the deceiving God and the evil demon (Med. 1).
column2:
Aim: extend doubt to arithmetic.
Premises: an all-powerful God could make me err even when I add two and three (AT VII 21); his goodness already permits some deception; if my author is fate or chance, error is likelier still; so every hypothesis about my origin gives a reason to doubt.
Conclusion: I must withhold assent from all my former beliefs. The evil genius (genius malignus, AT VII 22) adds no new reason; it keeps this one in view.
Objection (Hume, Enquiry XII): the doubt cannot be held, and if held it would be "entirely incurable".
Reply (Descartes' own, in part): it is "very slight, and so to speak metaphysical" (Med. 3, AT VII 36), concerns knowledge, not action, and lapses while I attend to a clear perception. See Argument 7.

column1: Reconstruct the cogito (Med. 2; Discourse IV; Principles I.7; Second Replies).
column2:
Premises: I am now thinking, since doubting and being deceived are cogitatio, which covers any conscious state; that I think cannot be doubted, because doubting is thinking; thinking needs something that thinks.
Conclusion: "I am, I exist, is necessarily true each time that I pronounce it, or that I mentally conceive it" (Med. 2, AT VII 25); so far, I am a thing that thinks. Descartes denies it is a syllogism (Second Replies, AT VII 140).
Objection: it claims too much. Hobbes: a thinking thing may be corporeal (AT VII 173); Lichtenberg: say only "it thinks".
Reply (Descartes' own, Third Replies, AT VII 174): whether the thinker is a body is settled only in Med. 6. Against Lichtenberg, the literature presses Descartes' substance principle (Williams). The dispute is open.

column1: Reconstruct the wax argument (Med. 2).
column2:
Premises: the wax after heating is the same wax; every sensory quality has changed; so what remains is known by no sense; it is "a certain extended thing which is flexible and movable" (Med. 2, AT VII 31); it can take more shapes than I can picture, so imagination cannot grasp it either.
Conclusion: bodies are perceived by the intellect alone, by an inspection (inspectio) of the mind; and the mind is known more clearly than any body.
Objection (Gassendi, Fifth Objections, AT VII 271–273): abstracting from the qualities leaves an unknown substratum, reached only by conjecture; Descartes' intellect is imagination of a kind.
Reply (Descartes' own, Fifth Replies, AT VII 359): he showed how the substance is manifested by its accidents; what stays is extension, the clearly understood nature of body.

column1: Reconstruct the trademark argument: objective reality and the causal adequacy principle (Med. 3).
column2:
Premises: I have an idea of God, an infinite substance; "there must at least be as much reality in the efficient and total cause as in its effect" (Med. 3, AT VII 40); this holds for the objective reality of ideas; my idea of God has infinite objective reality; nothing finite contains that reality, formally or eminently.
Conclusion: God exists as its cause, the workman's mark on his work (AT VII 51).
Objection (Gassendi; Hume): amplifying finite qualities builds the idea, so a finite mind is an adequate cause.
Reply (Descartes' own): the power of amplifying must itself have a source (Second Replies, AT VII 139; Fifth Replies, AT VII 365). Most modern readers reject the principle as applied to the content of ideas.

column1: Reconstruct the argument from my continued existence (Med. 3).
column2:
Premises: I exist, a thinking thing with the idea of God; I am not my own author, or I would doubt and desire nothing; the parts of time are independent, so something must conserve me at each moment, and "the distinction between creation and conservation is solely a distinction of the reason" (Med. 3, AT VII 49); I have no such power, or I would be conscious of it; my conserver has the perfections I have ideas of; a series of present conservers must end.
Conclusion: God exists and conserves me.
Objection (Gassendi, AT VII 300–301): many effects outlast their causes.
Reply (Descartes' own, AT VII 369–370): fathers cause only coming into being; God, like the sun with its light, causes being. The argument still rests on Argument 5's causal principle.

column1: Reconstruct the Cartesian circle and Descartes' reply (Fourth Objections and Replies; Second Replies).
column2:
Structure: the cogito yields the truth rule, which is doubted until God is proved; then "the certainty and truth of all knowledge depends alone on the knowledge of the true God" (Med. 5, AT VII 71).
Objection (Arnauld, Fourth Objections, AT VII 214): we are sure clear perceptions are true only because God exists, and sure God exists only because we clearly perceive it; so the proof presupposes its conclusion.
Reply (Descartes' own, Fourth Replies, AT VII 246; Second Replies, AT VII 140): present clear perception needs no guarantee; God is needed only for conclusions remembered without attending to their proofs.
Counter: Med. 3 doubts present perception too, and the proofs take time (Frankfurt, against Doney).
Readings (the literature's): refined memory; coherence (Gewirth, Frankfurt); rule-free (Van Cleve). There is no consensus.

column1: Reconstruct the argument that error comes from a will that outruns the intellect (Med. 4).
column2:
Premises: my intellect is finite; by my will I bear "the image and similitude of God" (Med. 4, AT VII 57); each faculty is good of its kind; error arises because "the will is much wider in its range and compass than the understanding" and I extend it to what I do not understand (AT VII 58).
Conclusion: God is not the author of my errors; I avoid them by withholding judgment where perception is not clear and distinct.
Objection: why give me a faculty that errs (Gassendi, AT VII 312)? And belief is not under the will's control (Spinoza; Williams).
Reply (Descartes' own, Fifth Replies, AT VII 376): liability to err is a lack, not a positive defect; the will reaches "Precisely to everything in which we happen to err".

column1: Reconstruct the ontological argument (Med. 5; Caterus; Gassendi).
column2:
Premises: what I clearly and distinctly perceive in a true and immutable nature can be affirmed of it; my idea of a supremely perfect being is such a nature, not a fiction; existence is a perfection; so existence can no more be separated from God's essence than angles equal to two right angles from a triangle (Med. 5, AT VII 66).
Conclusion: God exists; the necessity in the thing determines my thought (AT VII 67).
Objections: Caterus, after Aquinas: the concepts are joined, but nothing follows about the real world (AT VII 99). Gassendi: existence is not a perfection but the condition of every perfection (AT VII 323).
Reply (Descartes' own): only the idea of God contains necessary existence (First Replies); existence is a property as well as omnipotence (Fifth Replies, AT VII 382).

column1: Reconstruct the real distinction from clear and distinct conception (Med. 6; Second and Fourth Replies).
column2:
Premises: whatever I clearly and distinctly understand, God can make as I understand it; so things I clearly and distinctly apprehend apart can exist apart; I have a clear and distinct idea of myself as only thinking and unextended, and a distinct idea of body as only extended and unthinking (Med. 6, AT VII 78).
Conclusion: my mind is really distinct from my body and can exist without it.
Objection (Arnauld, Fourth Objections, AT VII 202): one may know that a triangle in a semicircle is right-angled without grasping Pythagoras' theorem; conceiving apart shows only thinking apart.
Reply (Descartes' own, Fourth Replies, AT VII 222–225): each must be understood as a complete thing, a substance, and the ratio is no complete thing. Disputed: Wilson argues the reply presupposes that thought is my whole essence.

column1: Reconstruct the divisibility argument (Med. 6).
column2:
Premises: every body is extended, so divisible at least in thought; considering myself only as a thinking thing, I find no parts; willing, feeling and understanding are faculties of one mind, not parts; losing a foot takes nothing from the mind.
Conclusion: "body is by nature always divisible, and the mind is entirely indivisible" (Med. 6, AT VII 86), so by Leibniz's law they are distinct. Descartes rates it sufficient only had he not learned this elsewhere.
Objections: premise 2 reports introspection, not structure; Kant's second paralogism: the unity of the "I think" is formal; split-brain cases (Nagel).
Reply (the literature's): it rests on Argument 10's result that the mind's essence is thought, and half a doubt makes no sense. Splitting can be assigned to the bodily machinery, which many find ad hoc.

column1: Reconstruct the proof of the external world (Med. 6).
column2:
Premises: I have a passive faculty of receiving sensory ideas; it would be useless without an active faculty producing them; that faculty is not in me, since the ideas come without my contribution, often against my will (Med. 6, AT VII 79); so it is in a body, God or a nobler creature; God gave me no faculty to recognise another cause, and a great inclination to believe bodies convey them; otherwise God would deceive.
Conclusion: "we must allow that corporeal things exist" (AT VII 80), perhaps not exactly as sensed.
Objections: Med. 3 distrusted natural impulses; Berkeley: matter is idle, God produces our ideas.
Reply (Descartes' text; the literature's on Berkeley): no faculty could correct this inclination, so a false one would make God a deceiver; Berkeley's God deceives in just that way.

column1: Reconstruct Elisabeth's interaction objection and Descartes' replies (letters of 1643).
column2:
Elisabeth (6/16 May 1643, AT III 661): moving a body needs contact or extension; the soul has neither; so how can a soul "being only a thinking substance" (my translation) move the spirits?
Descartes (21 May, AT III 665): there are primitive notions, extension for body, thought for soul, and their union; error explains one by another.
Elisabeth (10/20 June, AT III 685): it is easier to grant the soul matter and extension than an immaterial power to move a body.
Descartes (28 June, AT III 691–694): the union is known very clearly by the senses, through ordinary life.
Objection: "primitive notion" names the problem; the pineal gland only relocates it (Spinoza).
Reply (the literature's, divided): Cottingham's trialism takes the union as a third category; others hold that Descartes never answered.

column1: Reconstruct the argument that animals are machines: the language and action tests (Discourse V; letter to More, 1649).
column2:
Premises: a machine shaped like us could never arrange words to "reply appropriately to everything that may be said in its presence" (Discourse V, AT VI 56–57), nor act flexibly, since "reason is a universal instrument which can serve for all contingencies" (AT VI 57); humans pass both tests; animals fail, though parrots utter words.
Conclusion: animals have no reason; their behaviour is bodily mechanism, like a clock.
Objection: Montaigne and More: animals' signs of fear and cunning look like ours; and the tests detect only human-like reason.
Reply (Descartes' own, to More, 5 February 1649, AT V 276–278): mechanical explanation is more probable; he claims probability, not proof, and denies animals thought, not life or sensation that depends on a bodily organ. Turing later made the language test a criterion.

column1: Reconstruct the argument that matter is extension, so there is no vacuum (Principles II.4, 11, 16).
column2:
Premises: body's nature is not weight, hardness or colour, for if bodies always retreated from our hands we would feel no hardness, yet they would be bodies (Principles II.4); what remains is extension in length, breadth and depth, our idea of space (II.11); nothing has no properties, so wherever there is extension there is substance (II.16).
Conclusion: a vacuum is impossible; a vessel emptied of all body would have its sides touch (II.18). Hence no atoms, and a plenum.
Objections: Pascal's Puy-de-Dôme experiment (1648) left a space with no detectable matter; More: spirits are extended; Leibniz: extension needs force.
Reply (Descartes' own, then the literature's): subtler matter fills the space; the mind is extended only by its power (to More, AT V 347). Pascal won the physics; a physics of size, shape and motion survived.

column1: What is clear and distinct perception?
column2: Descartes' standard of knowledge. "I term that clear which is present and apparent to an attentive mind," as objects are seen clearly when they act strongly on the eye; the distinct is "so precise and different from all other objects that it contains within itself nothing but what is clear" (Principles I.45, AT VIIIA 22). Pain is clear but not distinct: vividly present, yet confused with a judgment that something like it exists in the foot (I.46). From the cogito Descartes draws the truth rule: "all things which I perceive very clearly and very distinctly are true" (Med. 3, AT VII 35). The rule awaits God's guarantee. Clarity belongs to intellectual perception, not to a feeling of certainty.

column1: What does cogitatio (thought) mean for Descartes?
column2: Cogitatio (French pensée) is far wider than reasoning. "Thought is a word that covers everything that exists in us in such a way that we are immediately conscious of it" (Second Replies, Def. I, AT VII 160): willing, understanding, imagining and sensing all count. A thinking thing doubts, understands, affirms, denies, wills, refuses, imagines and senses (Med. 2, AT VII 28). "Immediately" excludes bodily motions that follow from thought, so "I walk, hence I exist" holds only as awareness of walking (Fifth Replies, AT VII 352). The scholastics had put sensation in a sensitive soul shared with animals; Descartes makes consciousness the mark of the mental. Haldane and Ross sometimes render its parts misleadingly, as sentiens by "feels."

column1: What is the difference between formal and objective reality?
column2: Every idea can be taken two ways. As a mode of my mind it has formal reality, the reality anything has by existing, and in that respect all my ideas are equal. As a representation it has objective reality, the reality of what it represents: ideas of substances contain more than ideas of modes, and the idea of God more than any idea of a finite substance (Med. 3, AT VII 40). "Objective" means "as an object of thought," almost the reverse of today's sense. A cause contains a reality formally when it is the same kind of thing, eminently when it is something higher that could produce it, as God contains extension without being extended. The pair drives the trademark argument (Argument 5).

column1: What is the causal adequacy principle?
column2: The principle that "it is manifest by the natural light that there must at least be as much reality in the efficient and total cause as in its effect" (Med. 3, AT VII 40). Descartes extends it to ideas: an idea needs a cause "in which there is at least as much formal reality as this idea contains of objective reality" (AT VII 41), containing it formally or eminently. A regress of ideas must end in an archetype. The natural light is the mind's power to see such self-evident truths, distinct from the teaching of nature, which can mislead. The principle carries the trademark argument, the argument from conservation and the proof of bodies (Arguments 5, 6, 12). Most modern readers reject it as applied to the content of ideas.

column1: What are innate ideas, and how do they differ from adventitious and factitious ones?
column2: Meditation 3 sorts ideas into those that seem innate, adventitious and made by myself (innatae, adventitiae, a me ipso factae; AT VII 37–38). Innate ideas come from my own nature: thing, truth, thought, God. Adventitious ideas seem to come from outside, like a noise or the fire's heat. Factitious ideas are invented: sirens, hippogryphs. The sorting is provisional at that stage. What hangs on it shows in the sun: small as the senses show it, many times larger than the earth as astronomy, built from innate notions, shows it. Innate does not mean present at birth, as if infants thought about geometry. The Notes against a Programme (1648) compares innate ideas to family dispositions to certain diseases: a faculty that produces the idea on the right occasion.

column1: What is the doctrine of the creation of the eternal truths?
column2: A doctrine of the letters, not the Meditations. To Mersenne on 15 April 1630, Descartes wrote that the mathematical truths called eternal were established by God and depend on him entirely, like his other creatures (AT I 145); to make them independent is to treat God like Jupiter subject to the Styx, whereas he sets them as a king sets laws. On 6 May: in God willing and knowing are one (AT I 149). On 27 May: God is author of essences as "efficient and total cause" (AT I 152). In 1648 he told Arnauld he would not dare say God cannot make a mountain without a valley (AT V 224). This divine voluntarism strains against the fixed essences his proofs and physics need. Frankfurt and Curley read its force differently.

column1: What are a principal attribute and a mode?
column2: Substance is "an existent thing which requires nothing but itself in order to exist" (Principles I.51, AT VIIIA 24); strictly only God, while created substances need only his concurrence. We know a substance through its attributes, and "there is always one principal property of substance which constitutes its nature and essence, and on which all the others depend" (I.53, AT VIIIA 25): extension for body, thought for mind. A mode is a way a substance is, such as a shape or a volition, and cannot exist or be understood without it (I.56). God has attributes but no modes. A substance and its principal attribute differ only by a distinction of reason, so a mind that stopped thinking would be no mind. One attribute per substance makes dualism follow quickly.

column1: What is a real distinction?
column2: The Principles names three distinctions (I.60–62). A real distinction holds between substances, each clearly and distinctly understood without the other. A modal distinction holds between a mode and its substance, as between wax and its shape. A distinction of reason holds between aspects one thing has only in thought, such as a substance and its principal attribute. "Real distinction" is a technical term, not just "really different": it means the two can exist apart. Meditation 6 argues that mind and body are really distinct, because what I clearly and distinctly understand apart God can make exist apart (AT VII 78). Against Arnauld, the Fourth Replies add that each must be understood as a complete thing, a substance (AT VII 222).

column1: What are the three primitive notions?
column2: Replying to Elisabeth on 21 May 1643, Descartes named primitive notions (notions primitives), "as it were originals" on whose pattern we form all other knowledge (AT III 665). After the most general ones, being, number and duration, there are three: extension for body, from which shape and motion follow; thought for the soul; and the union of soul and body, on which depend the soul's power to move the body and the body's power to cause sensations and passions. Error comes from explaining one notion by another, as when we model the soul moving the body on one body pushing another (AT III 666). On 28 June he added the ways of knowing: soul by pure intellect, body by intellect aided by imagination, the union very clearly by the senses (AT III 691–692).

column1: What is the union of mind and body?
column2: Nature teaches "that I am not only lodged in my body as a pilot in a vessel, but that I am very closely united to it" (Med. 6, AT VII 81). A pilot sees damage to his ship; I feel pain. Pain, hunger and thirst are "certain confused modes of thought which are produced by the union and apparent intermingling of mind and body" (AT VII 81). They do not show how bodies are, but guide the composite toward what helps and away from what harms. To Elisabeth, Descartes said the union is learned by ordinary life and conversation and by abstaining from meditation (28 June 1643, AT III 692). Whether it is a third kind of thing is disputed: Cottingham's "Cartesian Trialism" (1985) says yes; most readers keep two substances.

column1: What are the animal spirits and the pineal gland?
column2: The Passions of the Soul (1649) locates mind-body interaction. The soul, though joined to the whole body, acts most immediately in "a certain very small gland which is situated in the middle of its substance" (Passions I.31, AT XI 351–352), the brain's. Descartes chose it because it is single, while most of the brain is double, so the images from the two eyes can meet there (I.32). The soul moves the gland slightly and so redirects the animal spirits (esprits animaux), the finest, fastest parts of the blood, which flow through the nerves and swell the muscles (I.34, AT XI 354). The spirits are bodies, not souls. The gland locates the interaction without explaining it: Elisabeth's question about contact applies to it as to any body.

column1: How does Descartes relate the will to judgment?
column2: Meditation 4 divides judgment between two faculties. The intellect perceives ideas and by itself neither affirms nor denies. The will (voluntas) affirms, denies, pursues and avoids; it is unlimited in scope and the chief image of God in us (AT VII 57). Judgment is an act of the will. That is new: Aquinas and most scholastics made judgment an act of the intellect, while Descartes makes belief something I do and answer for. Error comes from the mismatch, when I extend the will beyond what I clearly understand (AT VII 58), and the remedy is to suspend judgment there. The Principles draws the moral: free action is our chief perfection and the ground of praise and blame, for "we do not praise automatic machines" (I.37, AT VIIIA 18).

column1: What is the freedom of indifference, and how does Descartes rank it?
column2: Indifference is being moved to neither side for want of reasons. Meditation 4 says freedom does not need it: "the more I lean to the one," from clear reasons or because God so disposes my thought, "the more freely do I choose and embrace it," and indifference is "the lowest grade of liberty" (AT VII 57–58). Highest freedom is spontaneous assent to what is clearly seen. Letters to the Jesuit Mesland (2 May 1644, AT IV 110–120; one AT dates, with a query, 9 February 1645) seem to add a two-way power to hold back even from a clear truth, to show our freedom. Disputed: some read this as a power to turn attention away (Kenny discusses it); others see a change of view, perhaps after Jansen's Augustinus (1640).

column1: What does Descartes mean by matter as extension, and why is there no vacuum?
column2: The nature of body consists "solely in the fact that it is a substance extended in length, breadth and depth" (Principles II.4, AT VIIIA 42), not in hardness, weight or colour; hardness is only resistance to our hands. Space and body are one in reality. So "a space in which there is no substance" cannot exist, "because the extension of space or internal place, is not different from that of body" (II.16, AT VIIIA 49). An "empty" pitcher still holds air (II.17), and a vessel emptied of all body would have its sides touch (II.18). Further consequences: matter is indefinitely divisible, so no atoms (II.20), and the matter of heaven and earth is one, with no conceivable edge (II.21–22). All change is motion in a plenum.

column1: What are Descartes' laws of motion?
column2: Change is local motion, a part of matter passing from the neighbourhood of the bodies touching it to that of others (Principles II.25). God, being immutable, conserves the same total quantity of motion (II.36, AT VIIIA 61), and three laws follow. "The first law of nature: that each thing as far as in it lies, continues always in the same state; and that which is once moved always continues so to move" (II.37, AT VIIIA 62). The second: all motion is of itself in a straight line, so bodies moving in a circle tend to recede from the centre (II.39). The third governs collisions (II.40), with seven rules of impact, most of them false. The first two come close to Newton's inertia. In a full world motion is circular, whence the vortices.

column1: What is Descartes' tree of philosophy?
column2: In the 1647 Preface to the French Principles, a letter to its translator Claude Picot, Descartes wrote that "philosophy as a whole is like a tree whose roots are metaphysics, whose trunk is physics, and whose branches, which issue from this trunk, are all the other sciences" (AT IXB 14). The branches reduce to three: medicine, mechanics and morals, the last "the last degree of wisdom." The image makes three claims. Knowledge is one tree. Its order is fixed, metaphysics first because it holds the principles of knowledge. And its point is practical: fruit grows at the ends of the branches. The Discourse had promised to make us "masters and possessors of nature" (VI, AT VI 62), where the French hedges: comme, "as it were."

column1: What is the provisional morality?
column2: A man who pulls down his house to rebuild it needs somewhere to live meanwhile. So before doubting, Descartes formed "a code of morals for the time being" of three or four maxims (Discourse III, AT VI 22; une morale par provision). First, obey the laws and customs of his country and keep his childhood religion, following the most moderate opinions elsewhere. Second, be firm and resolute in action, like travellers lost in a forest who keep walking in one direction (AT VI 24–25). Third, "to try always to conquer myself rather than fortune" (AT VI 25), since only our thoughts are fully in our power, close to the Stoics. Fourth, cultivate his reason. Whether it stays temporary is disputed: Rutherford sees the late letters to Elisabeth developing it.

column1: What is generosity (générosité) for Descartes?
column2: Both a passion and a virtue, and the centre of Descartes' ethics in the Passions of the Soul (1649). The only good ground for self-esteem is "the use of our free will, and the empire which we possess over our wishes" (III.152, AT XI 445). True generosity consists partly in knowing that nothing truly belongs to us but this free disposition of the will, and partly in "a firm and constant resolution to use it well" (III.153, AT XI 445–446), never failing to undertake what we judge best. The generous do not despise others, believing everyone has the same free will (III.154). It is "the key of all other virtues" (III.161, AT XI 454). Not open-handedness with money. The will of Meditation 4 becomes the one thing fully ours.

column1: What is the Cartesian circle, as a problem for the system?
column2: The system makes God guarantee clear and distinct perception: the truth rule of Meditation 3 waits on proof that God exists and is no deceiver, and "the certainty and truth of all knowledge depends alone on the knowledge of the true God" (Med. 5, AT VII 71). But God is proved by clear and distinct perceptions. Mersenne first raised it (Second Objections, AT VII 124–125), adding the atheist geometer; Arnauld gave the classic form (Fourth Objections, AT VII 214). Descartes' answer separates present perception from memory (Fourth Replies, AT VII 246): God is needed for remembered conclusions, so the atheist's knowledge is not scientia, stable knowledge (Second Replies, AT VII 141). Whether this saves the structure is disputed (Argument 7).
